theses.title: The one-paragraph story
theses.text:
## The one-paragraph story

A predecessor system (not present in this repo) proved the concept and then
collapsed under its own success: roughly 140 accumulated feedback rules loaded
as prose pushed fresh sessions toward 400–500k tokens of always-on context,
where rules fired wrongly or vanished when needed most. In the project's RPG
vocabulary, it brought the **whole stash into every map** — as if a character
carried gear for every damage type when the encounter called only for cold
resistance. In plain language, irrelevant rules consumed attention and created
unintended interactions before the task began. The author's implementation
answers with _compiled_ rules: each correction becomes a typed mechanism (a
permission, a guard, a reactor, an evaluator, a transformer, a workflow gate)
attached only where relevant. A session in that profile gets **a build, not a
biography** — one active behavior, a handful of linked supports, its selected
safety layer, and the exact task state. The platform supplies the compiler and
mechanism contracts without prescribing that loadout. The [starter proof](../evidence/WO-118/README.md) completed resident-owned scratch delivery and review repair with writer replacement and resident restart; a fresh export demonstrated live status, while efficiency remains unmeasured.

theses.title: The core bet
theses.text:
## The core bet

> "The true work of the inventor consists in choosing among these combinations
> so as to eliminate the useless ones... the rules that must guide the choice
> are extremely fine and delicate. It's almost impossible to state them
> precisely; they must be felt rather than formulated." — Poincaré, via Pirsig

Generation is cheap and getting cheaper; the scarce asset is the **selection
function** — the operator's sense of what is good, currently exercised one
correction at a time. DotLn's bet is not that this delicate judgment can be
exhaustively formulated. It is that useful operational approximations can be
progressively arrived at: source incidents preserve what was felt, candidate
mechanisms approach it from different directions, and regression fixtures show
where each construction agrees or diverges. As mathematical or geometric
techniques can converge on a shape without becoming the shape itself, the
formulation is an instrument for approaching the operator's selection function,
not a claim to contain it precisely. **The model changes; the organization
survives.** Claude, Codex, a human, a shell script, and a future model are
interchangeable occupants of the same actor slot.

That bet needs an excellent foundation before it needs a long feature list. In
the reference implementation, the smallest useful loop—declare intent, see what
the system understood, observe authorized progress, receive timely feedback,
and inspect evidence—should already feel responsive, legible, and worth
repeating. Competitive gap-filling does not excuse a weak loop. When another
system introduces a useful idea, DotLn first asks whether the exact behavior can
be accommodated by existing primitives, compositions, ports, and runtime
lowerings. If not, the difference becomes evidence for one missing primitive or
boundary, not permission to bolt on an opaque special case. Integration and
semantic accommodation are preferred to imitation; both preserve every
capability contract the receiving implementation declares and expose any
omitted or lossy capability.

theses.title: The differentiated interface
theses.text:
## The differentiated interface

DotLn's second thesis is about _authoring_, not running:

> "I will take the entire Business, Leadership, and Personal Development shelf
> at Barnes & Noble and just map them to different agent / subagent
> communication structures... at once anyone who has read those books is an
> expert in some feature of the app — and it turns all those books into
> programming books overnight."

The analogies are not documentation — **the analogies are the ways you mix and
match the agents**. Every pattern (5S, the Ladder of Leadership, mitigated
speech, Theory of Constraints, commedia dell'arte roles, the
Algorithms-to-Live-By policies) compiles into exact mechanics, and the same
compiled program renders through an open-ended set of isomorphically equivalent
views: an RPG character with a Path-of-Exile-style socket-and-link build, a
business pattern card, a statechart, a function table, a marble/Morse temporal
track, a TypeScript DSL, an event timeline. Friendly metaphors are authoring
languages, never camouflage: every view either provably compiles to the same
normalized program or is labeled a lossy projection with the exact mechanics one
click away.

### Shape-first synthesis

The operator uses situations and analogies to communicate a desired **shape**: a
relationship, interaction, transition, contrast, feedback loop, or felt quality.
Literal similarity to the reference is not the acceptance test unless a specific
literal detail becomes load-bearing. Preserve the experience first, then
progressively lower it through observable interaction, domain mechanics,
contracts and evidence, and finally technology selected from representative
environment evidence. An imperfect analogy can carry a precise requirement;
source accidents do not become ontology by resemblance.

This is the standing interpretation rule for earlier and future operator
ideation. Its fullest product expression is the first-party application thesis,
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md), but it applies to the whole platform.

theses.title: Three horizons, one kernel
theses.text:
## Three horizons, one kernel

1. **Work operating system** — workstreams, disposable workers, evidence-backed
   completion, offline-capable state, a near-empty main thread. The immediate
   product.
2. **Executable pattern workshop** — the shelf-to-mechanism compiler and the
   drag-a-card-onto-an-agent authoring surface. The differentiated product.
3. **Agent ecology & simulation laboratory** — paired counterfactual runs,
   first-divergence detection, agent swaps, reflection-policy experiments over
   recorded event logs. The research product.

Horizon 3 must emerge from the same kernel (deterministic replay is what makes
counterfactuals possible at all) and is not allowed to distort Horizon 1.
The [workstream application candidate](12-workstream-application.md) develops
Horizon 1 through concrete end-user journeys and gradual workflow replacement,
including one outcome spanning multiple repositories. It leaves deployment and
application identity open and does not allocate another release rung.
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md) is the operator-named application destination that
joins Horizons 2 and 3: prose-authored patterns and ad hoc interventions become
playable inside an inspectable counterfactual community. Naming the destination
does not move it ahead of the release ladder or make its application-local
content kernel doctrine.

theses.title: Mission — increase the chance of operator flow
theses.text:
## Mission — increase the chance of operator flow

This is the mission of the author's personal implementation and a motivating
use of the platform, not a compulsory objective or operating policy for every
DotLn owner.

AI-assisted work commonly falls into a babysitting mode: the operator repeatedly
restates context, supplies procedural guidance, coordinates tools and workers,
checks unsupported completion claims, recovers stalled work, and spends active
attention on the machinery instead of the idea. The desired alternative is not
unbounded improvisation or confidence without evidence. It is a sustained
creative flow in which the operator can keep the idea and implementation
direction in mind while the surrounding work behaves dependably.

The reference implementation's mission is to improve the conditions for that
**operator flow state**.
Supporting research, capability-building, coordination, routine procedure,
recovery, and verification should happen automatically when authorized,
predictably when routine, and helpfully when a genuinely material decision needs
the operator. Product and research investment should favor capabilities that
remove recurring supervision and avoidable context switches without exporting
their cost into correctness, authority, evidence, privacy, or recoverability.

The implementation cannot promise or infer a person's psychological state. It can
reduce interruption, repetition, manual ceremony, and rediscovery; preserve
intent and working context across handoffs; package necessary interruptions as
decision-ready inputs; and make recovery unsurprising. Under its selected
profile, flow does not silently authorize scope expansion, skipped verification,
perpetual action, or self-certification. “Give an agent a build, not your
biography” remains useful architectural shorthand for one mechanism serving
this larger mission.

exclusions.text:
Not an agent, an agent harness, or an agent-orchestration layer, as its
  identity. DotLn is an **agentic platform**: the shared substrate on which
  people and software actors hold work, authority, and evidence. It contains an
  orchestration layer and hosts harnesses as observed environments
  ([runtime primitive catalogs](03-architecture.md#runtime-primitive-catalogs)),
  but neither of those is what it is.
Not a prompt library, and not a wrapper that makes one vendor's model nicer.

Not a prescribed catalog of ideal agents, roles, personalities, workflows, or
  organizational doctrine. Bundled patterns are examples and optional starting
  points, not kernel truth.

Not dependent on a public marketplace. Local files, private catalogs,
  organization-internal registries, and offline or air-gapped installations
  remain complete authoring and distribution paths.

Not one prescribed autonomy curve. Presence and recorded time are policy
  inputs; an explicit owner policy may hold, shrink, grow, peak, reset, or loop
  scope and authority within its declared ceiling.

In the reference implementation, not a metrics theater: no invented numbers,
  no activity-as-progress, evidence precedes "done," and utilization is not the
  objective. A profile that omits verification says so instead.

The reference implementation is not finished when it works for its author:
  v1.0 means a person who has never read these docs can declare a bounded intent
  and receive a verifiable result.

orders.title: WO-233 — DotLn cleans up after itself: an integration drops its own stash when it completes, every temporary root carries an owner and a retention class the prune judges, the prune runs inside release close, session end and gate end instead of in the operator's hands, a complete review reuses a warm export fixture instead of a fresh install per run, and the kit carries all of it to every instance (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
Nothing the lifecycle or the gate creates on a machine
outlives its use without a recorded owner and a retention class, and nothing
is ever handed to the operator to delete. An integration drops its own stash
when it completes; every temporary root is created through one helper that
records its owner, class and retention, and `harness prune` judges those
records; the prune runs where the lifecycle already runs, at release close,
at session end for the session's own trees and at gate end for the gate's
own fixtures, and its report is printed where a role would otherwise not
see it; a complete review reuses a warm export fixture keyed by the kit's
manifest and lockfile instead of installing into a fresh export per run,
and the gate records how many files it created and deleted and what the
host's file-event daemon weighed before and after; prune and gate serialize
under the host lock instead of refusing each other; read-only leftovers are
made writable before removal; and every piece ships in the kit, so an
instance that takes the release prunes its own residue and core's gate
proves it on the fixture instance with history.

orders.title: WO-234 — A dispatch cannot run away: every role session carries a wall-clock bound and a complete-run bound read from the budgets file, the gate, the bounded wrapper and the lifecycle refuse to start past it, the hooks say where the session stands at every turn, an operator acceptance extends it on the record, and the meter reports every stop and what followed (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
No dispatch runs past a bound the operator can read and
change. Each dispatch kind has a wall-clock bound and a complete-run bound
in the budgets file; the gate's host task refuses to start a complete or
review selection past either, the bounded wrapper refuses to start a probe,
the lifecycle refuses to re-dispatch the same phase, and under Claude the
hooks refuse a tool call that would start any of these, each naming the
bound, the standing and the two routes: `analysis:` to diagnose, or an
operator acceptance recorded by `npm run resume -- accept-overrun` with the
operator's captured words, which extends the bound for that order's phase
and nothing else. Focused reproductions (`--only`) and the lifecycle's
reads stay admitted, so a stop never locks out diagnosis. The Stop hook
prints the dispatch's standing at every turn so the operator sees the clock
without asking. The meter records every stop, every acceptance and the next
lifecycle event after each with its delay, and `plan failures` lists them,
so a planning pass reads whether a stop or an operator intervention helped,
which is the evaluation WO-192's D023 asked for, as data rather than as a
second lifecycle driver.

orders.objective:
Two duties become checks, and one standard replaces the
latest example.

- **Shape from the contract, not the predecessor.** Every generated role
  carries the rule: an artifact's shape comes from its contract and the
  check that judges it; a previous instance is evidence of what happened,
  never the pattern; when the contract is silent on a shape, say so in the
  record and keep the artifact to what the contract names. `plan start`
  writes the pass document's skeleton from product 07's artifact list, so a
  pass has no reason to open the previous one for its shape.
- **The standard is the best comparable, disclosed.** For each measured
  artifact class (pull-request body, order file, planning document,
  verification and final-review reports) the meter records the smallest
  passing instance of the same class over the last twenty closes as
  `bestComparableBytes` with the instance named and the ratio; completion,
  `plan start` and the planning receipt print the advisory ("8,594 bytes;
  best comparable passing 1,746, WO-222; 4.9 times; state the changed
  condition or shorten"); the writing guidance names the best comparable
  instead of the nearest example. No byte cap is set: ceilings are
  planning's, and the operator's direction of 2026-09-14 stands.
- **Every operator message is answered.** The prompt hook records each
  operator message in the dispatch with an index and a content digest; the
  role writes one direction-ledger entry per message, a typed record
  (`index`, `digest`, `event`, `aim`, `disposition`, `record`) whose
  `event` is the role's recorded judgment from the north-star set
  (`OperatorCorrectionReceived`, `OperatorReportsRepeatedFailure`,
  `OperatorRejectsUnsupportedAssumption`, `OperatorReportsRegression`,
  `OperatorReorder`, `OperatorDirection`, `OperatorAnswer`); completion
  (`implementation-ready`, `repair-complete`, `verification-result`,
  `final-review-result`) and `plan receipt` refuse while a recorded message
  has no entry, naming it. A later message adds to the earlier aim unless
  its entry records a withdrawal; the dispatch's aim stays first unless an
  `OperatorReorder` entry says otherwise.
- **A correction is heard at its urgency.** An entry whose event is a
  correction, a repeated-failure report or a rejected assumption triggers
  the compiled fail-conservative freeze whether or not the message carried
  a typed prefix: no scope expansion, no destructive effect, the aim stated
  in one line, the correction acted on before the role continues, the
  dispatch aim resumed in the operator's priority. A raised register is
  read as urgency on the same direction, never as new scope and never as a
  mood; the classification is the role's judgment, recorded, with the
  register as at most a weak feature (the ledger's rule).

orders.title: WO-207 — Instance update control: an instance takes kit machinery with its build pinned or followed, keeps its own code at a manifest-excluded extension root that the kit's machinery loads through the SourceAdapter port and no update touches, rolls back its last update to the prior kit state, and takes a starter update only through an upgrade order its own planning pass cuts, gated by kit conformance and its own declared suites (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
An instance controls the kit updates it takes, from core and
inside the instance:

- **Its own code.** `dotln.config.json` may declare `extensions`: a root
  outside every kit tree (default `extensions/`) and adapters by kind
  (`source`, `effect`, `projection`). A vertical issue naming
  `source: "<id>"` has `prepare()` load that adapter, record
  `ExtensionLoaded { id, kind, path, sha256 }` and call its `fetchBundle`
  in place of `fetchIssueBundle`, with the bundle passing the same checks
  as the GitHub source's; `effect` and `projection` adapters are admitted
  and listed, never imported here. No export, manifest or update touches
  the root; the README states the review burden. The first consumer is a
  fixture adapter; the enterprise-tracker adapter is the work instance's.
- **Its build.** The kit manifest names its build (the compiled definition
  modules, their semantic hash and compiler version). An update takes
  `both` (today's), `machinery` (build modules kept at their pinned bytes,
  `build.pin` recorded, emit, check and `kit-verify` honoring it) or `build`
  (the build alone, then the re-emit), and refuses an incompatible pairing
  before any write; inside an instance, the upgrade order runs
  `build --pin` or `build --take` after its merge, as the channel the
  operator chose. WO-076's overlay composes over whichever build is pinned.
- **Its way back.** Each update logs what it did and keeps retained copies,
  refusing before any write when it cannot. `rollback` inside the instance,
  or `export --update <dir> --rollback` from core, returns the kit files
  and manifest to the logged state before the last update, reverses the
  reversible instance actions (the update's `build.pin` among them), lists
  the rest by id, logs itself and prints the re-emit, which the role that
  ran it runs next; it refuses, naming the path or row, after a later kit
  edit, when the update is not the latest, or when a prior file has no
  verified source.
- **Its way in.** An instance takes a starter update through the session-run
  route the client README records since WO-210: the incoming revision
  previewed from a detached worktree of that revision, the merge on an update
  branch, the re-emit and lineage index, one commit, the push and the update
  pull request the operator merges (the personal fork took its #1, #3, #8 and
  #16 this way). For the operator's instances the upgrade order a planning
  pass (dedicated, or part of one) cuts from the kit's template is that
  route's recorded form: it names the starter revision, the channel and each
  refused path's resolution, carries the route as its plan, runs the channel's
  `build` form after the merge and passes the gate below; the template's
  rollback form takes the way back the same way. A planning branch writes only
  `docs/` and root Markdown (WO-135), so the pass never applies kit files.
- **Its gate.** The consumer selection WO-213 decided (WO-213-D014: the six
  structural tasks and `kit-verify`, run fresh; carried kit suites stay
  explicit `--only` and `--machinery` diagnostics) plus the instance's own
  additions, the planner's proposal (assumption 8): suites it declares in
  `dotln.config.json` `suites` (name, command and sources), selected by
  changed sources, appended to that selection and run fresh, with each
  extension adapter naming the suite that covers it. Core's own gate is
  unchanged.
- **No step is the operator's by hand.** The operator gives the word (the
  starter revision, the channel, how each refused path resolves, a
  rollback), types the dispatch phrases and merges the pull request; a
  role runs every command and makes every commit (operator direction,
  2026-10-13; planning document §12.1).

criteria.text:
An `extensions` section with a root under a kit tree, a symlinked root,
   an uncontained module, a duplicate id, an unknown kind, or an adapter
   whose `suite` names no declared suite or a suite whose `sources` omit
   its module refuses naming the key, and an absent section loads as the
   default root with no adapters; a `suites` entry with a duplicate or
   non-lowercase name, an empty or non-string `command` or an uncontained
   source refuses naming the key, and an absent section loads as none; a
   `build.channel` outside the three, or a malformed `build.pin`, refuses
   naming the key, and an absent channel reads as `both` (configuration
   cases).

The fixture vertical runs from intake to contract with an issue naming
   `source: "fixture"`: the adapter's bundle passes
   `requireCompleteIssueBundle`, the screen and `decodeSourceBundle` as the
   GitHub source's does, and the record the decisions name holds
   `ExtensionLoaded` with the module's SHA-256; an undeclared id refuses at
   configuration; a wrong export shape refuses naming the id (vertical and
   extension cases).

Declared `effect` and `projection` adapters are listed by kind with
   their contained paths and SHA-256 and never imported (their top-level
   markers stay absent after listing and after a vertical run); no consumer
   runs them (extension cases).

An export from a core checkout carries no path under the extension root
   and the manifest lists none; in a fixture instance an update leaves the
   root byte-identical and refuses a planted kit path inside it (launchpad
   cases).

The kit manifest (schema 2) names its build files as the relative-import
   closure of `contributor.js` and `feedback.js` inside
   `packages/skeleton/dist/src/loadouts/` (six files at `926b8234`), its
   semantic hash and compiler package version; a schema 1 manifest reads as
   all machinery (fixture).

Under `machinery` an update replaces every kit file but the build
   modules, which keep their pinned bytes, records `build.pin` and leaves
   the emitted bundle at the pinned build after the re-emit; under `build`
   only the build modules change and the re-emit produces the new build
   over unchanged machinery; under `both` the plan equals today's; the
   preview shows the partition and the channel in each case (fixture).

The from-core preview and the update's summary label and count
   byte-identical replace rows `unchanged`, with `planUpdate`'s kinds, the
   writes and the receipt unchanged; the in-instance revision preview lists
   an absent manifest-listed kit path the incoming manifest still carries as
   a local-removal row (unchanged upstream when its incoming and prior
   hashes match), prints every other row and declared action and exits 0,
   while the from-core preview and the update still refuse it before any
   write (fixture).

A `machinery` update whose incoming compiler is incompatible with the
   pin, and a `build` update whose definitions are incompatible with the
   installed compiler, refuse before any write and print the two choices;
   compatibility is the Design's guard (the major from 1.0, the minor below
   it, every imported name present in the pinned modules, every name a pinned
   module imports still exported by the machinery module outside `build.files`
   that it imports); a channel or pin
   beside an overlay's `build: "none"` refuses before any emit or update
   write (fixture).

`harness emit` from a pinned build produces the pinned revision's
   bundle; `harness check` passes with the pin and refuses a pinned module
   whose bytes differ (fixture).

In a fixture instance that merged a starter revision, `build --pin`
    restores and verifies the pinned modules from its history,
    `build --take` adopts the merged modules and moves the pin, each prints
    the re-emit instruction, and both refuse when the history lacks the
    pinned blobs; after `build --pin`, `node scripts/launchpad.mjs verify`
    passes on the pinned modules and still refuses any other differing
    `packages/<name>/dist/` file (fixture).

An overlay composed over a pinned build equals its composition at the
    pinned revision (fixture).

An update appends one log row (the prior and new commits, the prior
    manifest, the new manifest's hash, the pre-update commit or null, the
    channel, the plan, the applied actions) and retains a copy of each file
    it replaces with different bytes or removes, none for a byte-identical
    replacement, with no retained copy in `git status`; with the lane or
    the log unwritable it refuses before any write, naming the path
    (fixture).

A rollback after an update restores every kit file to the prior
    manifest's hash and the prior manifest, removes added files, restores
    removed ones, and leaves every instance file byte-identical (fixture).

Reversible actions are reversed (`rename-root`, `add-config-field` the
    update added, `change-phrase`, a `build.pin` the update wrote) and an
    action in an unexpected state is listed by id with the file to edit,
    not guessed (fixture).

The rollback refuses, writing nothing and naming the path or row, after
    a later kit edit, with no newer update above the last rollback, and when
    a prior file is restorable from neither source; with a committed prior
    and no retained copy it restores from Git and verifies the hash
    (fixture).

The from-core and in-instance forms produce byte-identical trees, each
    appending a `rollback` row and writing no receipt in core; a fork that
    merged a starter revision rolls back from the merged row through the
    pre-update commit, or refuses naming the row; a rollback after a
    `machinery` or `build` update restores what its plan listed and the
    prior `build` section (fixture).

The instance's own suites (the planner's proposal, assumption 8): a
    declared suite runs when a path changed against the merge base lies under
    its `sources` and not otherwise; a missing merge base selects no declared
    suite, the consumer default unchanged, unless the decisions file records
    an operator-approved exception to product 07 §Preflight before the full
    gate; `--only <name>` runs it; its failure fails the gate; a name equal to
    a kit row refuses (runner fixtures).

The kit carries `scripts/kit/upgrade-order.template.md`,
    manifest-listed; filled on an exported instance's planning branch, it
    indexes as an Open order and the branch changes no path outside
    `docs/`; its plan previews the revision through that revision's own launchpad from
    a detached `.runtime/upstream-preview` worktree before it merges on the
    order's branch, runs the channel's `build` form, re-emits and checks the
    harness, indexes lineage, verifies the kit, and runs `npm test` and `npm
    run test:docs`; its rollback form runs `rollback` and the same checks; the
    `dotln-step-roles` block gives every numbered step a role from the fixed
    set and only the pull-request merge maps to `operator`; a schema-1 fixture
    instance previews a schema-2 starter revision that way while its own
    launchpad refuses the manifest (launchpad and launchpad-planning cases).

The client README's §Taking upstream updates documents the log, the
    retained copies, the fail-closed refusal, both rollback forms, the
    reversals and refusals, the re-emit, the unchanged rows, the revision
    preview's local-removal row, the channel section and the way in (the session-run update pull request,
    with the channel's build form after the merge, and the upgrade order a
    planning pass cuts as its recorded form for the operator's instances;
    every command a role's, on the operator's word, with nothing left to
    resolve or commit by hand; the route kept for an instance owner without an
    order); its
    §Instance extensions states the root, the registration, the `source`
    contract, the record, the unimported kinds, the covering suite and the

## Goal-aligned decisions

The Contributor's purpose comes from [the vision](00-vision.md): DotLn is a
local-first, model-agnostic compiler/runtime for human judgment. This personal
implementation aims to improve operator flow by moving recurring supervision,
coordination, recovery and verification into dependable machinery, while
preserving correctness, authority, evidence, privacy and recoverability.

The current [critical-path plan](../planning/critical-path-2026-09-08.md) targets
the always-on runtime, its first real external source change and an independently
verified source-to-deliverable loop.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

**Platform lens.** Four checks from the platforms lesson the operator
pointed at (Steve Yegge's 2011 account of the Amazon service mandate) apply
to any capability a plan or order lands: it arrives as an interface
something else consumes (a transport profile, a typed event, a projection, a
handoff packet), never only as a script or a session; it is externalizable
by construction (content-addressed inputs, declared contracts, no private
setting as the source of a guarantee); this repository and the operator's
own repository consume it before any export; and its result is usable by a
stranger to the session, so a receipt that needs reverse-engineering is an
accessibility failure [[vision-into-use pass](../planning/vision-into-use-2026-09-17.md)
§12, 2026-09-17]. The planning refuter's platform-first standard is
unchanged.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

The shared supports carry these duties and their compiled identity in both
harnesses. They are instruction-level judgment, not proof that an agent applied
every lens or a causal detector. The meter's five quantitative trap signals are
separate. General Naive Interventionism, NoOp and adaptive Tinkerer mechanics
retain their candidate scope; this bounded Contributor policy does not claim
their generalized implementations. The [WO-043 receipt](../evidence/WO-043/ideation-commands-and-usage.md)
records this promotion and its limits.

To check claims the orders make, I opened these read-only at the base: .claude/settings.json (hooks), .claude/hooks/finish.mjs (head), packages/skeleton/src/harness-host.ts (hook events, Stop handling, session scratch, and the prompt hook's OperatorMessageObserved record), scripts/lib/harness-prune.mjs (apply path and session-end judgment), scripts/lib/worktree-integration.mjs (stash handling), scripts/release.mjs (cleanup blockers), scripts/test-runner.mjs (machinerySources and the launchpad row), docs/control/budgets.json (head), scripts/lib/process-budget.mjs (validation) and scripts/test-fixture-temp-root.sh (head). orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No row of the supplied critical-path table names WO-233. The sequence places it first, ahead of WO-192 and WO-083 (gate P, the fork's run), and the vision records gate V's starter proof (WO-118) as completed. Its supplied text names no gate it unblocks. The nearest named outcomes are the kit clause (an instance that takes the release prunes its own residue, proven on the instance-history fixture) and the removal of D084's `Prune subject changed` refusal that stopped the operator's chain. I read it as risk-reduction prerequisite work for P; that is an inference from the sequence and the objective, not a stated dependency. NoOp cost, as the Cost line records it: the residue regrows and the operator deletes it by hand (85 integration stashes, 41.30 GB; 641 session scratch trees, 9.7 GB; 24,526 `dotln-*` temp roots, 14 GB, the oldest from 2026-09-29; WO-192-D081, D084). Every complete review also keeps paying an `npm ci` per export fixture after the first (export task 164.231 s at WO-216's base; plain-gate thirty-day median 419.1 s against a 360 s threshold). The supplied cost-table observations carry no disk-residue series, and WO-192's cited decisions are not committed at base 6e7f01da (git ls-files lists no docs/evidence/WO-192), so a stranger cannot check this baseline from the base. The refusal the order targets is real at base: harness-prune.mjs line 859 throws `Prune subject changed` when an apply-time re-check differs. Action beats NoOp because the residue is recurring operator rescue (the shifting-the-burden lens).
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: it adds one structural refusal (raw `mkdtempSync` in the `declarations` task) and a prune-beside-gate path that criterion 7 lets end in refusal. Observed guardRefusals were 0,0,0,1,1 across WO-230..WO-204; bypassTools and adHocScripts are null, so workaround pressure is unmeasured. Tragedy of the commons: this is the main benefit, about 65 GB of shared disk residue and per-run installs removed. It also adds a per-gate census (filesCreated, filesDeleted, bytesWritten), a gate-end prune and an fseventsd sample to a gate already above its threshold (419.1 s median against 360 s), and the Wall-clock line does not cost any of them. Drift to low performance: no role-text change is planned. Executor (29,827 > 29,246) and reviewer (29,584 > 28,884) are already in breach (drift-to-low-performance observation), and the order commits to recording before and after bytes if it must touch contributor.ts. Product 07 grows. Escalation: 16 steps and 14 criteria across integration, prune, release, hooks, gate, launchpad, budgets, kit, instance history and four documents. Criterion 2's every-root rule covers 361 tracked `mkdtempSync(` calls in 131 tracked files at base (git grep: scripts 253 in 82, packages 101 in 42, corpus 7 in 7), and the Cost line does not count them. Three of the last eight orders failed first verification (WO-219, WO-232, WO-204), and breadth raises the odds that an auxiliary criterion holds the whole order. Success to the successful: it extends `harness prune`, but the alternatives (one per-session parent removed whole, OS temp expiry) are not recorded. An owner marker already exists, `.dotln-test-root-owner` written by scripts/test-temp-root.sh (sourced by 9 scripts), and the new owner record does not name it, which risks two owner formats. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: positive. It removes handed-off cleanup commands, and criterion 13 makes the executor run them. Residual risk: a prune failure becomes a cleanup blocker with a `Retry:` line (release.mjs), which under a host denial goes back to the operator. Rule beating: the declarations check names only raw `mkdtempSync`, so child-process temp roots (npm, git) and other creation forms escape it; zero async `mkdtemp` or `mkdirSync(tmpdir())` sites exist at base. Criterion 7 can pass by refusing. Seeking the wrong goal: it targets operator flow (manual cleanup, chain stops, install time) rather than a proxy, and the fseventsd figure is explicitly a measurement, not a pass mark.
orders.removalBalance: Yes, on the measured axes. Removals the Cost line names: about 65 GB of recurring residue (41.30 + 9.7 + 14 GB), the cleanup commands handed to the operator (D081, D084), D084's chain-stopping refusal, and every export-fixture `npm ci` after the first. Additions: one module, three candidate kinds, three lifecycle placements, retention keys, and seconds of prune at release close and session end (the dry run judged 84.8 MB in under a second). Not quantified on the addition side: the migration of 361 call sites (review and read cost), the gate-end prune and census time, and an owner-record write for every temporary root. Tokens are unknown. Net wall-clock stays unknown until criterion 8 measures it; net operator attention and disk favour removal. One factual error at base: the Cost line says `launchpad-fixture.mjs` is a declared source in `machinerySources`, but scripts/test-runner.mjs lists it only in the `launchpad` nodeTests row's sources (line 1055), and `launchpad` is not a `machinerySources` key. Its `npm test -- --review` conclusion still holds, because harness-prune.mjs, test-runner.mjs and test-launchpad-export.mjs are machinery sources.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades to the old behavior. An interrupted stash application keeps the stash (criterion 1). A release-close prune failure becomes a cleanup blocker, which release.mjs records as advisory (`Advisory: ... cleanup blocker`), so the residue simply stays. A failing suite's roots stay tagged, and an absent retention block reads as the seeds. There are three exceptions. (a) Criterion 7 admits a refusal where the objective promises serialization instead of refusal, so D084's stop can come back under another name. (b) The declarations refusal is a deliberate new gate refusal. (c) Criterion 5's self-removal does not degrade. The Claude hooks registered in .claude/settings.json include Stop and no SessionEnd; harness-host.ts accepts no SessionEnd event and documents a Stop as ending the turn, and WO-234 relies on Stop firing every turn. So 'at session end' in criterion 5 means every turn end at which the writer is released and no background dispatch runs. The session is live at its own Stop, which contradicts criterion 3's live-owner rule and the existing prune's own session-end judgment (harness-prune.mjs around line 509 requires a dead owner and a finished Stop). A misjudgment there deletes live working state instead of leaving residue.

findings.reason: Criterion 5 places the session-end prune in the Claude Stop hook, but Stop fires at the end of every turn, not at session end. On a multi-turn session with its writer released and no background dispatch, the hook would remove the session's own scratch tree and worker captures between turns, while the session (live by criterion 3's own rule) still holds the path printed to it as its working root. Removal doesn't fall back to the old behavior: it loses state the next turn may need, such as a staged prompt or a result file awaiting receipt. The existing prune deliberately refuses a session root until the owner is dead and a finished Stop is journaled.

findings.reason: The objective promises that prune and gate serialize under the host lock instead of refusing each other, and the Cost line claims the removal of D084's chain-stopping refusal. Criterion 7, though, passes on 'waits or refuses naming the gate' and 'waits or refuses naming the prune'. A refusal-only implementation would satisfy the criterion while the operator's chain still stops, only under a new message.

findings.reason: Criterion 2's every-root rule implies migrating 361 tracked `mkdtempSync(` calls in 131 tracked files, and the Cost line neither counts nor names that migration. A second owner format would also appear beside the existing `.dotln-test-root-owner` marker that scripts/test-temp-root.sh writes, and the order doesn't say whether the new helper adopts or replaces it. The scope raises first-verification risk (3 of the last 8 orders failed first verification), and two formats would leave the prune judging owners by two rules.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No row of the supplied critical-path table names WO-234. The sequence places it second, before WO-192 (one session drives an order through its lifecycle) and WO-083 (gate P, whose fork run 'drives it through its lifecycle the way core drives orders at that time'). Its text names what it guards: WO-192's runaway phase, and the stop-evaluation WO-192's D023 asked for, supplied as data rather than as a second lifecycle driver. That makes it risk reduction for WO-192 and, through it, gate P, an inference from the sequence and WO-083's title. NoOp cost, as the Cost line records it: one WO-192 phase ran 80,817,117 ms of executor wall clock, 327,404,836 tokens, 109 gate steps and 17,144,915 ms of gate time with no phase transition, stopped twice by the operator and never by the system (WO-192 meta.json, D076, D084). Under NoOp the operator's attendance stays the only stop for the next driven run. Those WO-192 records are not committed at base 6e7f01da, so I could not check the figures here, and the supplied observations carry no per-dispatch wall-clock series. Action beats NoOp because WO-192 follows it directly in the sequence.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the sixth refusal at four sites (gate host task, bounded wrapper, lifecycle re-dispatch, Claude hooks). Observed guardRefusals were 0,0,0,1,1, and bypassTools and adHocScripts are unmeasured. If the seeds are tight, roles will route through the admitted `--only` reproductions. Tragedy of the commons: it targets the commons directly (gate time and, through wall clock, tokens), though tokens stay unbounded by non-goal. Drift to low performance: it adds a shared sentence to every role root, and criterion 9 grows the generated CLAUDE.md paragraph to six refusals with Codex and Copilot rows. CLAUDE.md counts in every root's cold-start bytes (the acceptances cite 'CLAUDE.md 6,873 plus the skill'), so both additions land on executor and reviewer roots already in breach (29,827 > 29,246; 29,584 > 28,884). The Cost line counts only the shared sentence, and criterion 8 records before and after bytes without the same-change raise or dated acceptance that the standing direction in docs/control/budgets.json requires ('never left advisory across orders'). Escalation: one refusal brings an operator command, an event, three meter fields and a plan-failures block. That is bounded, since an acceptance extends only one order's phase. Success to the successful: it reuses the budgets file, the session journal and the meter, which is good. Active-time or token bounds are credible alternatives; token bounds are excluded by non-goal, and active versus elapsed time is not addressed. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: stops move from operator attendance to the system, which is positive. But every stop needs an operator acceptance with captured words that the executor is refused, so a false stop (for example, idle time on an attended session paused overnight) adds operator rescue. Rule beating: past the bound, `--only` selections and edits stay admitted, so a dispatch can keep looping on focused runs without tripping the complete-run counter. The bound limits complete runs and probes, not the session. Seeking the wrong goal: it aims at the outcome (no runaway) and produces the evaluation data D023 asked for.
orders.removalBalance: Yes, by the order's own numbers. It removes the exposure measured in one 22.4 h executor phase with 327 M tokens and 4.8 h of gate time, and it removes operator attendance as the only stop. It adds milliseconds of reads per gate start, probe start and turn end, one operator command, one event, meter fields, a shared role sentence and a larger generated CLAUDE.md paragraph. The removal caps a tail risk with one observed instance (WO-192); it is not a saving each order realises. The permanent context-byte addition to every role is under-counted, because the Cost line omits the CLAUDE.md growth. Tokens are unknown. Whether the cap repays its permanent context cost depends on how often runaways recur, and with one instance on record that rate is unknown.
orders.failureBehavior: By design the mechanism refuses. Absent configuration degrades: an absent key reads as `null`, which gives `unset` and today's behavior. Diagnosis stays open through `--only`, reads, `analysis:` and `operator override:`, and under Codex, which is unhooked, the gate, wrapper and lifecycle refusals still apply. What happens when the mechanism's own inputs fail is unspecified. Criterion 2 lists a missing-journal case without naming its result. If a missing or unreadable journal or gate-row read yields `exceeded`, or throws inside the gate's host task, every complete run refuses. That is a mechanism failure that refuses instead of degrading. Separately, the stop is not total: a dispatch past its bound can continue with admitted focused runs, so a runaway can carry on in a narrower shape until the lifecycle refuses the next re-dispatch.

findings.reason: `dispatchStanding` has a case for a missing journal, but no supplied text says the result is `unset`. If unreadable inputs produce `exceeded` or an exception, the gate's host task, the bounded wrapper and the lifecycle all refuse, turning a bookkeeping fault into a full stop that needs an operator acceptance. Absent keys already degrade to `null`, and unreadable inputs should degrade the same way.
findings.reopenWhen: A gate row, bounded-wrapper refusal or lifecycle refusal names the dispatch bound for a dispatch whose session journal or gate rows were missing or unreadable at the check.

findings.reason: The bound is wall-clock elapsed since dispatch start, read from the session journal, and nothing separates active work from idle time. An attended session paused for hours (the operator away, the presence policy idle) would be refused at its next complete run though nothing ran away, and each such false stop costs an operator acceptance with captured words. The seeds' basis is left to the decisions, so whether the seed accounts for idle time is unknown.

findings.reason: Past the bound, focused `--only` selections, reads and edits stay admitted, so the refusal stops complete runs and probes, not the dispatch. A runaway like WO-192's (109 gate steps in one phase) could keep looping on focused runs until the lifecycle refuses the next re-dispatch. The Stop hook shows the standing but doesn't stop anything.
